readings.c1s3:
¶
'''In no wise''', in no way; on no account; by no means.

{{smaller block|Merlin hem comaunded that, as soone as thei were arived at the porte, ''in no wise'' that thei tarye not but two dayes.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 420.}}
Ower patrone of the shippe had sent to hym letters at Candy that he shuld toche at the rodes ''in no wysse.''
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 22.}}
<poem>
He is promised to be wived
To fair Marina; but ''in no wise''
Till he had done his sacrifice.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, v. 2. 11.}}
A simple, ill-bred zealot, exceedingly vain, but ''in nowise'' coveting riches or gain of any sort.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 205.}}}}

'''On this wise''', in this way or manner.

{{smaller block|<poem>
Than was it schorter than the assise,
Thrise wroght thai with it ''on this wise;''
Accorde to that werk wald it noght.
</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 80.}}
''On this wise'' ye shall bless the children of Israel.
{{right|Num. vi. 23.}}}}

'''To make wise†''', to make pretense; pretend; feign; sham.

{{smaller block|Or as others do to ''make wise'' they be poore when they be riche, to shunne thereby the publicke charges.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 252.}}}}

¶
'''-wise.''' An apparent suffix, really the noun ''wise''<sup>2</sup> used in adverbial phrases originally with a preposition, as in ''anywise'', ''nowise'', ''likewise'', ''otherwise'', etc., originally ''in any wise'', ''in no wise'', ''in like wise'', ''in other wise'', etc.; so ''sidewise'', ''lengthwise'', etc., in which, in colloquial use, ''-ways'' also appears, by confusion with ''way''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wiseacre''' (wī′zā-kėr), ''n.'' [= MD. ''wijssegger'', < G. ''weissager'', soothsayer, < ''weissagen'', MHG. ''wīssagen'', OHG. ''wīzagōn'', ''wīzzagōn'', foretell, predict, < ''wīzago'', ''wīzzago'', a prophet, diviner (AS. ''witega'', ''witiga'', prophet): see ''witch''. The MHG. verb and noun became confused with ''wīs'', wise, and ''sagen'', say, and the E. noun is likewise vaguely associated with ''wise''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' A sayer of wise things; a learned or wise man.

{{smaller block|Pythagoras learned much, . . . becoming a mighty ''wiseacre''.
{{right|''Leland.''}}}}
'''2.''' One who makes pretensions to great wisdom; hence, in contempt or irony, a would-be wise person; a serious simpleton or dunce.

{{smaller block|There were at that time on the bench of justices many Sir Paul Eithersides, hard, unfeeling, superstitious ''wiseacres''.
{{right|''Gifford'', note to B. Jonson’s Devil is an Ass, v. 5.}}}}

¶
{{smaller block|And yet this Libertine is crown’d for the Man of Merit, has his ''Wishes'' thrown into his Lap, and makes the Happy Exit. {{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 143.}}}}

'''wish''' (wish), ''v.'' [< ME. ''wisshen'', ''wysshen'', ''wischen'', ''wuschen'', < AS. ''wȳscan'', less correctly ''wiscan'' = MD. ''wunschen'', ''wenschen'', D. ''wenschen'' = MLG. ''wunschen'' = OHG. ''wunsken'', MHG. G. ''wünschen'', wish, desire, = Icel. ''æskja'' (for ''œskja'') = Sw. ''önska'' = Dan. ''önske'', wish; all orig. from the noun, though the mod. E. word has the vowel of the verb: see ''wish'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To have a wish or desire; cherish some desire, either for what is or for what is not supposed to be obtainable; long: often with ''for'' before an object.
{{smaller block|They cast four anchors out of the stern, and ''wished for'' the day. {{right|Acts xxvii. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
But if yourself . . .
Did ever . . .
''Wish'' chastely and love dearly.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, i. 3. 218.}}}}
{{smaller block|This is as good an argument as an antiquary could ''wish for.'' {{right|''Arbuthnot'', Ancient Coins, p. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Those potentates who do not ''wish'' well to his affairs have shewn respect to his personal character. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To desire; crave; covet; want; long for: as, what do you ''wish?'' my master ''wishes'' to speak with you.
{{smaller block|<poem>
I goe with gladnesse to my ''wished'' rest.
</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Daphnaïda, l. 282.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
The dredfull beast, ycleped crocodile, . . .
Before he doth devoure his ''wished'' prey,
Pitty in outward semblance doth display.
</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 22.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
I would not ''wish'' them to a fairer death.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 8. 49.}}}}

fidence, approval, kindness, or care.

{{smaller block|If I can by any means light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will ''wish'' him to her father.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 1. 113.}}}}

{{smaller block|Sir, I have a kinsman I could willingly ''wish'' to your service, if you will deign to accept of him.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}

'''To wish one further.''' See ''further.''

'''wishable''' (wish′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''wish'' + ''-able.''] Worthy or capable of being wished for; desirable. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The glad ''wishable'' tidinges of saluacion.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Luke iv.}}}}

'''wishbone''' (wish′bōn), ''n.'' The furcula, or merrythought of a fowl. Also ''wishing-bone.''

'''wishedly†''' (wish′ed-li), ''adv.'' [< ''wished'', pp. of ''wish'', + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] According to one’s wish. ''Knolles.''

'''wisher''' (wish′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''wish'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who wishes.

{{smaller block|''Wishers'' were ever fools. ''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 15. 37.}}

'''wishful''' (wish′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''wish'' + ''-ful.'' Cf. ''wistful.''] '''1.''' Having or expressing a wish; desirous; longing; covetous; wistful.

{{smaller block|<poem>From Scotland am I stol’n even of pure love,
To greet mine own land with my ''wishful'' sight.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 14.}}
<poem>On Jordan’s stormy banks I stand,
And cast a ''wishful'' eye
To Canaan’s fair and happy land,
Where my possessions lie.</poem>
{{right|''S. Stennett'', The Promised Land (Lyra Britannica, ed. 1867, [p. 527).}}}}

{{smaller block|I pray you tell where the ''wise'' man the conjuror dwells.
{{right|''Peele'', Old Wives’ Tale.}}}}

{{smaller block|They are ''wise'' to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.
{{right|Jer. iv. 22.}}}}

<poem>In these nice sharp quillets of the law,
Good faith, I am no ''wiser'' than a daw.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 4. 18.}}}}

'''5.''' Religious; pious; godly.

{{smaller block|From a child thou hast known the holy Scriptures, which are able to make thee ''wise'' unto salvation.
{{right|2 Tim. iii. 15.}}}}

'''6.''' Dictated, directed, or guided by wisdom; containing wisdom; judicious: as, a ''wise'' saying; a ''wise'' scheme or plan; ''wise'' conduct or direction; a ''wise'' determination.

<poem>The justice . . .
Full of ''wise'' saws and modern instances.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 156.}}}}

<poem>May, . . . spite of praise and scorn, . . .
Attain the ''wise'' indifference of the wise.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Dedication.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Never the wiser,''' without information or advice; still in utter ignorance.}}

{{smaller block|The Pretender, or Duke of Cambridge, may both be landed, and I ''never the wiser''.
{{right|''Swift'', To Miss Vanhomrigh, June 8, 1714.}}}}

{{smaller|'''The seven wise men of Greece,''' the seven sages. See ''sage''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''—'''To make it wise†,''' to make it a matter of deliberation.}}

{{smaller block|Us thoughte it was noght worth to ''make it wys.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 785.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Wise woman.''' (''a'') A woman skilled in hidden arts; a witch; a fortune-teller.}}

<poem>They call her a ''wise-woman'', but I think her</poem>
An arrant witch. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}
<poem>Supposing, according to popular fame,
''Wise woman'' and Witch to be the same.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Tale of a Trumpet.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') A midwife.   ''Scott.''}} ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Sagacious, discerning, oracular, long-headed. See ''wisdom''.—'''6.''' Sound, solid, philosophical.}}

'''wise<sup>2</sup>''' (wīz), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wise'', ''wyse'', < AS. ''wise'' = OS. ''wisa'' = OFries. ''wis'' = D. ''wijs'' = LG. ''wise'' = OHG. ''wisa'', MHG. ''wise'', G. ''weise'' = Icel. *''vis'' (in comp. ''öthruvis'', otherwise) = Sw. Dan. ''vis'', way, manner, wise; from the same source as ''wise''<sup>1</sup>: see ''wise''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''-wise''. Doublet of ''guise''.]   Way; manner; mode; guise; style: now seldom used as an independent word, except in such phrases as ''in any wise'', ''in no wise'', ''on this wise''.
{{smaller block|<poem>This Troilus, in ''wyse'' of curteysie,
With hauk on hond and with an huge route
Of knyghtes, rood and dide hire compaynye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 64.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ther-vpon a while I stood musyng,
and in my self gretly ymagynyng
What ''wise'' I sholde parfourme this seid processe.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 52.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whan Dodynell herde these tithinges, he seide to hymself that he wolde do the same ''wise'', and tolde to his prevy counseile that he wolde go to court.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|So turne they still about, and change in restlesse ''wise''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VII. vii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|I considered myself as in some ''wise'' of ecclesiastical dignity. {{right|''Swift'', Mem. of P. P.}}}}
'''In any wise''', {{smaller|in any way; by any means.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Now, for my loue, helpe that I may hir see
''In eny wise'',” quod Auferius the kyng;
“ffor I canne think right wele that it is she.”</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1241.}}}}

{{smaller block|A simple, ill-bred zealot, exceedingly vain, but ''in nowise'' coveting riches or gain of any sort.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 205.}}}}

{{smaller block|{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|''On this wise'' ye shall bless the children of Israel.
{{right|Num. vi. 23.}}}}

The MHG. verb and noun became confused with ''wīs'', wise, and ''sagen'', say, and the E. noun is likewise vaguely associated with ''wise''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' '''wise-hearted''' (wīz′här″ted), ''a.'' Wise; knowing; skilful. Ex. xxviii. 3.

'''wise-like''' (wīz′līk), ''a.'' Resembling that which is wise or sensible; judicious; sensible. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|The only ''wise-like'' thing I heard anybody say. {{right|''Scott.''}}}}

'''wiseling†''' (wīz′ling), ''n.''   [< ''wise''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who pretends to be wise; a wiseacre.
{{smaller block|This may well put to the blush those ''wiselings'' that show themselves fools in so speaking.
{{right|''Donne'', Hist. Septuagint, p. 214.}}}}

'''wisely''' (wīz′li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wisliche'', ''wislike'', wisely, < AS. ''wīslīce'', wisely; as ''wise''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wise manner; with wisdom, cunning, or skill; judiciously; prudently; discreetly. Prov. xvi. 20.
{{smaller block|The heorte is wel iloked ȝif muth and eien and earen ''wisliche'' beoth ilokene. {{right|''Ancren Riwle'', p. 104.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let us deal ''wisely'' with them; lest they multiply, . . . and fight against us. {{right|Ex. i. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then must you speak
Of one that loved not ''wisely'' but too well.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2. 344.}}}}

'''wisen†''', ''a.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete spelling of ''wizen''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wiseness''' (wīz′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wisnesse'', < AS. ''wīsness''; as ''wise''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.]   Wisdom.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet have I something in me dangerous,
Which let thy ''wiseness'' fear.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1. 286.}}}}

'''wiserine''' (wiz′ėr-in), ''n.''   [Named after D. F. ''Wiser'' (born 1802), a Swiss mineralogist.]   A rare mineral found in Switzerland in minute yellow octahedral crystals. It was long referred to xenotime, but has since been shown to be a variety of octahedrite (anatase).

'''wish''' (wish), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wisch'', ''wyssche'', a var., after the verb, of ''wusch'', < AS. ''wūsc'' = MD. ''wunsch'', ''wensch'', D. ''wensch'' = OHG. ''wunsc'', MHG. G. ''wunsch'' = Icel. ''ōsk'' (cf. Sw. ''önskan'' = Dan. ''önske''), wish, desire; see the verb, and cf. Skt. √ ''vāñchh'', wish; perhaps a desiderative form (with formative ''-sk'', as in E. ''ask''), from the root of E. ''win'', etc., strive after: see ''win''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Desire; sometimes, eager desire or longing.
{{smaller block|Behold, I am according to thy ''wish'' in God’s stead.
{{right|Job xxxiii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy ''wish'' was father, Harry, to that thought.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 93.}}}}
{{smaller block|The whole essence of true gentle-breeding (one does not like to say gentility) lies in the ''wish'' and the art to be agreeable.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vi.}}}}
'''2.''' An expression of desire; a request; a petition; sometimes, an expression of either a benevolent or a malevolent disposition toward others.
{{smaller block|<poem>I thank you for your ''wish'', and am well pleased
To wish it back on you.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 4. 43.}}
Delay no longer, speak your ''wish'',
Seeing I must go to-day.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}</poem>}}
'''3.''' The thing desired; the object of desire.
{{smaller block|That faire Lady schal zeven him, whan he hathe don, the first ''Wyssche'' that he wil wyssche of erthely thinges.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 145.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You have your ''wish''; my will is even this.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 2. 93.}}</poem>}}

{{smaller block|And yet this Libertine is crown’d for the Man of Merit, has his ''Wishes'' thrown into his Lap, and makes the Happy Exit. {{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 143.}}}}

'''wish''' (wish), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wisshen'', ''wysshen'', ''wischen'', ''wuschen'', < AS. ''wȳscan'', less correctly ''wiscan'' = MD. ''wunschen'', ''wenschen'', D. ''wenschen'' = MLG. ''wunschen'' = OHG. ''wunsken'', MHG. G. ''wünschen'', wish, desire, = Icel. ''æskja'' (for ''œskja'') = Sw. ''önska'' = Dan. ''önske'', wish; all orig. from the noun, though the mod. E. word has the vowel of the verb: see ''wish'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' </poem>

{{smaller block|This is as good an argument as an antiquary could ''wish for.'' {{right|''Arbuthnot'', Ancient Coins, p. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Those potentates who do not ''wish'' well to his affairs have shewn respect to his personal character. {{right|''Addison.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To desire; crave; covet; want; long for: as, what do you ''wish?'' my master ''wishes'' to speak with you.

{{right|''Spenser'', Daphnaïda, l. 282.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>

{{smaller block|<poem>
I would not ''wish'' them to a fairer death.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 8. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|They may be Patrons, but there are but few Examples of Erudition among them. ’Tis to be ''wisht'' that they exceeded others in Merit, as they do in Birth.
{{right|''Lister'', Journey to Paris, p. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Spartan ''wish’d'' the second place to gain,
And great Ulysses wish’d, nor wish’d in vain.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, x. 274.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Mortals whose pleasures are their only care
First ''wish'' to be impos’d on, and then are.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Progress of Error, l. 290.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Here’s news from Paternoster Row;
How mad I was when first I learnt it!
They would not take my Book, and now
I ''wish'' to goodness I had burnt it.</poem>
{{right|''F. Locker'', Old Letters.}}}}
'''2.''' To desire (something) to be: with objective predicate.
{{smaller block|For the wynde was thanne better in our waye thanne it was at any tyme syns we come frome Jaffe, and was so good that we coude not ''wysshe'' it better.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|I believe, as cold a night as ’tis, he could ''wish'' himself in Thames up to the neck.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 1. 120.}}}}
{{smaller block|Is it well to ''wish'' thee happy?
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
'''3.''' To desire in behalf of some one or something (expressed by dative); invoke, or call down (upon): as, to ''wish'' one joy or luck.
{{smaller block|Let them be driven backward and put to shame that ''wish'' me evil. Ps. xl. 14.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If heaven have any grievous plague in store
Exceeding those that I can ''wish'' upon thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 3. 218.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All joys and hopes forsake me! all men’s malice,
And all the plagues they can inflict, I ''wish'' it,
Fall thick upon me!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iii. 2.}}}}
'''4†.''' To recommend; commend to another’s confidence, approval, kindness, or care.

{{smaller block|If I can by any means light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will ''wish'' him to her father.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 1. 113.}}}}

{{smaller block|Sir, I have a kinsman I could willingly ''wish'' to your service, if you will deign to accept of him.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}

'''To wish one further.''' See ''further.''

'''wishable''' (wish′a̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ''wish'' + ''-able.'']   Worthy or capable of being wished for; desirable. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The glad ''wishable'' tidinges of saluacion.
{{right|''J. Udall'', On Luke iv.}}}}

'''wishbone''' (wish′bōn), ''n.'' The furcula, or merrythought of a fowl. Also ''wishing-bone.''

'''wishedly†''' (wish′ed-li), ''adv.''   [< ''wished'', pp. of ''wish'', + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   According to one’s wish.   ''Knolles.''

'''wisher''' (wish′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wish'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who wishes.

{{smaller block|''Wishers'' were ever fools.
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 15. 37.}}}}

'''wishful''' (wish′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''wish'' + ''-ful.'' Cf. ''wistful.'']   '''1.''' Having or expressing a wish; desirous; longing; covetous; wistful.

<poem>From Scotland am I stol’n even of pure love,
To greet mine own land with my ''wishful'' sight.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 14.}}}}
<poem>On Jordan’s stormy banks I stand,
And cast a ''wishful'' eye
To Canaan’s fair and happy land,
Where my possessions lie.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''S. Stennett'', The Promised Land (Lyra Britannica, ed. 1867, [p. 527).}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
